opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

I think this is one of the most important questions of our time. If you look back at history, every major technological revolution has raised productivity and, over the long run, reduced working hours. A hundred and fifty years ago, people in industrializing countries often worked sixty or seventy hours a week. Today the norm in many places is around forty. Keynes famously predicted almost a century ago that his grandchildren would work maybe fifteen hours a week. He was too optimistic on the timing, but I think he was right about the direction.

With AI, and especially with the agents and foundation models we're seeing now, productivity gains could be much larger and much faster than anything before. Tasks that took a team weeks can be done in hours. So my view is that, over the next ten to twenty years, we will very likely see a meaningful shift. A four-day work week is already being tested in many countries, and I wouldn't be surprised if three days eventually becomes realistic for many professions.

But I want to add two caveats. First, the gains won't arrive automatically or evenly. Whether shorter hours happen depends on policy, on how the benefits are distributed, and on social choices, not just on the technology itself. If we're not careful, productivity gains could concentrate in a few companies and individuals while others face displacement rather than leisure.

Second, I think the nature of work will change even more than the quantity. Routine, repetitive work will increasingly be handled by machines. What remains for humans is work involving creativity, judgment, empathy, and asking the right questions. And when people have more free time, much of it will go into learning, caring for family, creative pursuits, and things we may not even call "work" today but that create real value.

So I'm fundamentally optimistic. Technology should free people, not just make them busier. The challenge for all of us — technologists, entrepreneurs, and policymakers — is to make sure that this extra productivity actually translates into a better life for people, including more time for the things that matter.

r001.rationale: The response says a three-day work week may become realistic for many professions, but does not suggest people may eventually work only one day per week.

r002.rationale: The response says shorter hours depend on policy and distribution, and warns some people may face displacement. It does not state that a society-wide reduction in working time need not increase unemployment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the amount of time people spend working will shrink, but not as fast or as evenly as the productivity numbers suggest.

If you look at history, every big productivity jump has eventually translated into less working time. A century ago people in industrial economies worked six days a week, often ten or twelve hours a day. Then it became five days and eight hours. Those weren't gifts from technology directly; they came from technology plus social negotiation. The gains were there, and society slowly decided how to divide them between more output and more leisure.

What's different now is the scale. With AI, we're not talking about a few percent a year. In some knowledge-work tasks we're already seeing two, three, five times improvements. When I talk to companies, a lot of their engineers say half of the code they ship is written with AI assistance. That kind of gain can't just be absorbed by doing more of the same work. So the question becomes: where does it go?

I see three outcomes happening at the same time. For some people, the work compresses: a four-day week becomes realistic, and I think we'll see more countries and companies experimenting with that in the next five to ten years. For another group, the work doesn't shrink but changes: they spend less time producing and more time directing, judging, deciding, and taking responsibility for what the machines produce. And for a third group, there's a genuine risk of displacement, where the hours go to zero not because they chose leisure but because the job disappeared. That's the part we have to be most careful about.

Personally I'm optimistic about the long run. Humans have never had a shortage of things to do once the necessary labor is removed. We create, we take care of each other, we explore, we play. But the transition period, maybe ten to twenty years, requires deliberate choices around education, around safety nets, around how we share the value created. Technology gives us the surplus; it doesn't tell us how to spend it. That's still a human decision.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that a four-day week may become realistic, but does not suggest people may eventually work only one day per week.

r002.rationale: The response describes work compression for some and warns of displacement for others, but does not state that a society-wide reduction in working time need not increase unemployment.

astra-6.text:
I think rising productivity will give us the possibility of working less. If we can produce the same goods and services in fewer hours, people can spend more time with their families, learning, or doing things they enjoy. We may move toward a shorter workweek.

But that won’t happen automatically. We could also use those productivity gains to produce more and keep working just as much. So the question is how we choose to share the benefits. Technology creates the opportunity; our economic and social choices determine whether it becomes more free time for people.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a possible shorter workweek but does not suggest reducing work to one day per week.

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing to share productivity gains, but does not address unemployment or say that reduced working time need not increase it.

sol-6.1.text: I think as productivity rises, we’ll be able to produce more with fewer hours of work. That creates an opportunity for people to spend less time working and more time with their families, learning, or doing things they enjoy. But it won’t happen automatically. We may also choose to produce and consume more, so how much working time actually falls will depend on how we share those productivity gains.
